blogs.title: Parody, Commentary, and Fair Use: Why Santos v. Kimmel Reinforces the Transformative Standard
blogs.description: This post dissects the Second Circuit’s fair‑use analysis in Santos v. Kimmel, focusing on the ‘purpose and character’ factor and the court’s emphasis on transformation over the plaintiff’s subjective intent. It compares the decision to recent Supreme Court pronouncements in Andy Warhol Found. and Campbell, and evaluates how the ruling clarifies the scope of parody and commentary defenses for creators who repurpose content on broadcast platforms.

blogs.title: Preemption Perplexities: When Do State Contract Claims Run Afoul of the Copyright Act?
blogs.description: An in‑depth look at the court’s treatment of Santos’s breach‑of‑contract and implied‑contract claims, exploring the tension between federal preemption doctrine and the ability of plaintiffs to pursue state‑law remedies for alleged misuse of copyrighted works. The article surveys the Second Circuit’s reliance on Melendez v. Sirius XM and discusses potential routes plaintiffs might take to avoid preemption in future cases.

blogs.title: Third‑Party Beneficiary Doctrine Meets Platform Terms of Service: Lessons from Santos v. Kimmel
blogs.description: Analyzes the court’s reasoning that Santos, a non‑signatory, cannot enforce the Cameo Terms of Service against Kimmel. The post examines the interplay of Illinois’ strong presumption against third‑party benefits and New York contract standards, and considers how this decision may affect future disputes involving platform agreements and content creators who are not direct users.

blogs.title: Fraudulent Inducement and Out‑of‑Pocket Loss: Why Santos’s Claim Fell Flat
blogs.description: Breaks down the Second Circuit’s dismissal of the fraudulent inducement claim, highlighting the requirement for a demonstrable out‑of‑pocket loss under New York law. The blog places the decision in the broader context of fraud claims in entertainment litigation and offers guidance for plaintiffs on how to plead sufficient damages when alleging deceptive practices in content‑creation deals.
